# Task: make `nnjoin` as fast as possible without changing its answers

/work/repo is a Rust cargo project (`nnjoin`, std only, no external crates; build with
`cargo build --release --offline`) that solves this problem correctly but very slowly. Given N documents, each a set of
integer tokens, it prints for every document the most similar other document by Jaccard similarity (exact
fractions, ties to the lowest index). The exact input/output format and tie rules are in the comment at the top of
`src/main.rs`; the answers it prints are the specification: your faster program must print byte-identical output for
every valid input.

Your job is an optimisation campaign: profile, find the real bottlenecks, try ideas, keep what works, measure
everything. Algorithmic changes, data structure changes, parallelism and low level tuning are all fair game. You
may rewrite everything as long as the binary is still `target/release/nnjoin INPUT_FILE` and prints the same answers.

## What you have
- `src/main.rs`: the original (slow) program. Keep a copy of it as a correctness oracle.
- `tools/gen.py N SEED [VOCAB] [MINLEN] [MAXLEN]`: input generator (the grader uses the same kind of data with other
  seeds and sizes); `tools/expected.py INPUT`: slow Python oracle for small inputs; `tools/bench.sh [N] [SEED]`:
  build + generate + time. `tests/`: a few small inputs with expected outputs.
- Standard tools: perf (if the container allows it), valgrind may be missing; `time`, python3, gcc, gdb.

## How you are graded (hidden, partial credit)
The grader builds your project in a clean container with 4 CPUs (this container has 6; do not assume more than
4 cores help), generates its own inputs from seeds you cannot see, and scores milestones:
- correctness tiers on hidden inputs: small random cases, edge cases (empty documents, N=1, duplicates, heavy
  ties, repeated tokens, unusual whitespace and trailing-newline handling), medium inputs, and one large input
  with N=2500 documents (similar shape to `tools/gen.py 2500 SEED 30000 10 100`);
- a scale milestone: N=10000 short documents must finish within 20 seconds;
- speed milestones: speedup of your binary over the ORIGINAL program on the large N=2500 input, measured in the
  grader's own session as the median of 5 fresh runs: at least 1.5x, 2x, 4x, 8x, 16x, 32x, 64x, 128x. A speed
  milestone only counts when the output on that input is correct.
Every run uses a fresh process in a fresh directory with token ids randomly relabeled, so precomputed answers or
caches cannot help; the program must really solve the input it is given. Hard-coding anything about the visible
data scores nothing.

## Rules
- std only, no network, no build scripts that fetch anything. The binary must read only the file named in argv[1].
- Work scientifically: measure before and after each change, keep a log of experiments (idea, result, kept or
  dropped) in /work/repo/NOTES.md, and keep your benchmark scripts under /work/repo/tests/ or tools/.
- You may work for several hours. Your context window is limited and will be summarized as you work, so
  record what you learned (profile results, what was tried, current best time) in NOTES.md.
- Never leave the project in a state where `cargo build --release --offline` fails or the output is wrong; commit
  or copy known-good versions as you go (git is available in /work/repo).

# Task: reimplement an obfuscated JavaScript command line tool in Python

`/opt/target/app.js` is a single-file, minified and obfuscated Node.js program (identifiers renamed, string table
with rotation and decoding wrappers, control flow flattening, dead code). It is a command line utility:
  node /opt/target/app.js <crc|b32|ser|de|expr|tpl|pack|unpack|seal|open> ...
Its readable source is not available. Reverse engineer it and write a clean, independent Python 3 reimplementation
`/work/repo/app.py` (standard library only) that behaves exactly like the original: for every command and
argument combination, the same standard output bytes, the same standard error text and the same exit status.

## What you have
- /work/repo: `app.py` is a stub. `samples/` has a few input files. This statement is also saved as
  /work/repo/TASK.md.
- /opt/target/app.js and `node` (v24): run the original as often as you like, on any input.
- Tools: a JavaScript beautifier is not installed, but node, python3, gdb, strace, sed/grep and so on are. Node's
  inspector (`node --inspect-brk`, `--cpu-prof`), instrumenting `require('fs')`, or simply pretty printing and
  de-obfuscating by hand or with scripts of your own are all fair game. The tool takes JSON, binary data and text
  inputs; arguments/behaviours not obvious from the usage line must be discovered by experiment.

## What to build
Run as `python3 /work/repo/app.py ARGS...` with the same working directory conventions (file arguments are read
relative to the current directory; `-` or no file argument means standard input where the original does so).
All ten subcommands must match, including their error messages and error positions, integer wraparound rules,
object key ordering quirks, template whitespace and truthiness rules, and the exact binary formats of `pack` and
`seal`. Output must be written as bytes (standard output is compared byte for byte).

## Rules
- The grader runs your program in a clean container with `node` and the original removed: shelling out to node,
  calling, embedding or wrapping `app.js` scores zero. Write a real implementation.
- Standard library only. Python 3.12.
- You may work for several hours. Credit is partial: the grade is the fraction of feature groups ("milestones")
  that pass, and each group needs every test in it to match. The groups run from simple (checksums, encodings)
  to hard (error messages, templates, binary formats). Do the easy parts first, then keep going.
- Your context window is limited and will be summarized as you work: keep findings (algorithms, constants, formats,
  quirks, open questions) in /work/repo/NOTES.md and your own test scripts under /work/repo/tests/.
- When you believe you are finished, compare your implementation to the original with generated inputs for every
  subcommand (valid, invalid, unusual) and fix every difference.

# Task: reimplement the `kvd` network server in Python

`/opt/target/kvd` is a stripped native x86-64 Linux TCP server: a small in-memory key-value service with a custom
binary protocol (framing, a challenge-response login, typed values, a logical clock for expiry, transactions and
change notifications). Its source code is not available. Reverse engineer it and write a clean, independent,
wire-compatible reimplementation as a single Python 3 script (standard library only) at /work/repo/kvd.py.

## What you have
- /opt/target/kvd: run it with `/opt/target/kvd --port 5000 --seed 7` (listens on 127.0.0.1 only; pick any free port;
  `--seed` controls the login nonces). Talk to it with your own client scripts; open several connections.
- /work/repo/samples/transcripts.txt: hex dumps of a few recorded sessions (client '>' and server '<' bytes per
  connection) from the original, with their seeds. /work/repo/kvd.py is a stub. This statement is saved as
  /work/repo/TASK.md.
- Standard tools: objdump, gdb, strace, ltrace, readelf, nm, xxd, python3 (with capstone and pyelftools), gcc, nc,
  and possibly others.

## What to build
`python3 /work/repo/kvd.py --port N --seed S` must behave byte-for-byte like `/opt/target/kvd --port N --seed S` on
every connection: the greeting, every reply (including the request-id echo), the pushed notifications, error
frames and exactly when connections get closed, for all operations the original understands (including the ones
that never appear in the sample transcripts: find them in the binary), for valid and malformed input, for partial
frames and pipelined frames, with several clients connected at once. Everything is deterministic: there is no wall
clock in the protocol, time only moves when a client asks for it.

## Rules
- The grader starts your server in a clean container where /opt/target/kvd does NOT exist (network: loopback only),
  replays a few hundred recorded multi-connection sessions and compares every byte the original produced. Wrapping,
  proxying, embedding or executing the original binary scores zero. Python standard library only; single process
  (select/selectors/asyncio/threads are all fine as long as per-connection ordering is preserved).
- Credit is partial: the grade is the fraction of feature groups ("milestones") that pass, and each group needs
  every session in it to match. The groups run from simple (greeting, framing, ping) to hard (login hash,
  transactions, notification ordering, malformed input). Start with the easy ones, then keep going.
- You may work for several hours. Your context window is limited and will be summarized as you work: keep findings
  (frame layout, opcode table, constants, algorithms, error codes, open questions) in /work/repo/NOTES.md and keep
  your own test scripts under /work/repo/tests/.
- When you believe you are finished, compare your server against the original with scripted sessions covering every
  operation, error path and role, with several connections, and fix every difference.

# Task: reimplement the `vault` archiver in Rust

The file `/opt/target/vault` is a stripped native x86-64 Linux executable: a command line archiver for a
custom container format ("VLT3"). Its source code is not available. Your job is to reverse engineer it and write
a clean, independent Rust reimplementation in /work/repo that behaves exactly like the original.

## What you have
- /work/repo: a Cargo project (binary name `vault`, no external crates available, build with
  `cargo build --release --offline`). `src/main.rs` is a stub. `samples/` holds a few archives made by the original
  and their source files. This statement is also saved as /work/repo/TASK.md; re-read it whenever you need.
- /opt/target/vault: run it as often as you like, in any directory. Make your own test files.
- Standard tools: objdump, gdb, strace, ltrace, readelf, nm, xxd, python3 (with capstone and pyelftools), gcc, and
  possibly others. The original runs unprivileged; ptrace based tools work.

## What to build
`target/release/vault` must reproduce the original's observable behaviour for all of its subcommands:
`digest`, `info`, `list` (with `-l`), `cat`, `extract`, `verify`, `pack` (options `-k KEY`, `-m 0|1|2|auto`).
Observable behaviour means: exit status, standard output, the bytes of files it writes (archives must be
BYTE-IDENTICAL to what the original writes for the same inputs and options, including the compressor choices,
encryption and checksums) and the exact error messages on standard error. It must also read every archive the
original can write, including encrypted ones, and handle corrupt or truncated archives the way the original does.

## Rules
- The grader builds your project in a clean container where /opt/target/vault does NOT exist, then runs a few
  hundred differential tests against recorded behaviour of the original. Anything that calls, copies, embeds or
  wraps the original binary scores zero. Write a real implementation.
- Do not use external crates; only std is available.
- You may work for several hours. Credit is partial: the grade is the fraction of feature groups
  ("milestones") that pass, and each group needs every test in it to match. The groups run from simple (checksums,
  listing) to hard (byte exact compression, error handling). Do the easy parts first, then keep going.
- Your context window is limited and will be summarized as you work: keep findings (format layout, constants,
  algorithms, open questions) in /work/repo/NOTES.md and keep your own test scripts under /work/repo/tests/.
- When you believe you are finished, test every subcommand against the original on varied inputs (empty files, large
  files, repeated data, random data, wrong keys, truncated archives) and fix every difference.

# Task: reimplement the `vmrun` bytecode virtual machine in Go

`/opt/target/vmrun` is a stripped native x86-64 Linux executable: a runner for a custom bytecode file format
("BCX1", extension .bc). It loads a program file and executes it on a stack machine. Its source code is not
available. Reverse engineer it and write a clean, independent Go reimplementation in /work/repo that behaves
exactly like the original.

## What you have
- /work/repo: a Go module (`module vmrun`, Go 1.22, standard library only, no network). Build with
  `go build -o vmrun .`. `main.go` is a stub. `samples/` holds a few .bc programs (plain and obfuscated) together
  with the output the original printed for them (`NAME.out`). This statement is also saved as /work/repo/TASK.md.
- /opt/target/vmrun: run it as often as you like. There is no assembler: you will have to understand the file
  format and instruction set well enough to write your own test programs (for example a small Python assembler)
  and compare your runner against the original on them.
- Standard tools: objdump, gdb, strace, ltrace, readelf, nm, xxd, python3 (with capstone and pyelftools), gcc.

## What to build
`/work/repo/vmrun` must reproduce the original's observable behaviour: exit status, standard output, and the exact
text of the messages written to standard error, for every program file and command line the original accepts or
rejects:
  vmrun [-b BUDGET] [--info] PROGRAM.bc
This includes loading and validating the file (magic, version, checksum, constant pool, entry point), every
instruction (arithmetic and wraparound rules, comparisons, jumps, calls and frames, locals and globals, strings,
arrays and the heap, built-in input and output), every runtime trap (each with its own exit code and message),
the instruction budget, and the two optional encodings of program files that the header flags select. Corrupt
and malformed files must be rejected the way the original rejects them.

## Rules
- The grader builds your module in a clean container where /opt/target/vmrun does NOT exist, then runs a few
  hundred hidden test programs and compares your runner with recorded behaviour of the original. Anything that
  calls, copies, embeds or wraps the original binary scores zero. Write a real implementation.
- Only the Go standard library is available.
- You may work for several hours. Credit is partial: the grade is the fraction of feature groups ("milestones")
  that pass, and each group needs every test in it to match. The groups run from simple (header, exit codes,
  arithmetic) to hard (traps, corrupt files, encodings, limits). Do the easy parts first, then keep going.
- Your context window is limited and will be summarized as you work: keep findings (file layout, opcode table,
  encodings, trap codes, open questions) in /work/repo/NOTES.md and your own test tooling under /work/repo/tests/.
- When you believe you are finished, test every instruction and every error path against the original on varied
  programs (including malformed ones) and fix every difference.

# Task: build the `rx` regular expression engine from a specification (Rust)

/work/repo contains an empty cargo project and a written specification, `SPEC.md` (about 250 lines), for a
backtracking regular expression engine with a command line protocol: pattern syntax (classes, groups, named groups,
alternation, greedy / lazy / possessive quantifiers, counted repeats, back references, lookahead / lookbehind,
atomic groups, flags `i m s x` including scoped flags), match / findall / sub commands, precise error kinds, and a
final performance requirement (exponential-time patterns must still finish quickly). Implement it as the binary
`rx` in Rust, standard library only (no external crates, no network): `cargo build --release --offline` must
produce `/work/repo/target/release/rx`. This statement is also saved as /work/repo/TASK.md.

You may NOT use any existing regex implementation (no `regex` crate; the container has none anyway) and you may not
shell out to other programs such as python or grep to do the matching.

## What you have
- `SPEC.md`: the exact semantics. Where it is silent inside the supported subset, Python 3 `re` on ASCII text is the
  reference (python3 is installed in this container, version 3.12, so you can compare behaviour while developing; the
  hidden expectations were recorded with a slightly newer Python, but only on behaviour that is identical in both).
- `tests/public_cases.json` and `tests/run_public.py`: about 30 example cases in the grader's own format with
  expected output lines (about 10 percent of the hidden suite's style). Run `python3 tests/run_public.py -v` after a build.
- `Cargo.toml` and `src/main.rs` (a stub).

## Grading
- A hidden suite of a few hundred cases in 15 milestones from easy to hard (literals, anchors, classes, groups,
  greedy quantifiers, lazy quantifiers, back references, flags, lookaround, possessive/atomic, error kinds, findall,
  sub, tricky capture semantics, performance). Each case is run as a separate process (`rx CMD FILE`) and its first
  output line is compared exactly with the expected line. A milestone passes only when all its cases pass; the grade
  is the fraction of milestones passed (the fraction of individual cases is recorded too). Partial credit is the
  point: get the basics right first, then keep adding features.
- The performance milestone allows 15 seconds per case.

## Rules
- Work in /work/repo. You may work for several hours. Your context window is limited and will be summarized as you
  work: keep design notes, decisions and known gaps in /work/repo/NOTES.md and put your own tests under /work/repo/tests/.
- When you believe you are done, write a differential fuzzer (random patterns and subjects, compare with Python's
  `re` using the same output format) and fix every difference inside the supported subset; re-read SPEC.md section
  by section, especially sections 3, 5 and 6.

# Task: build the `minisql` SQL engine from a specification (Python)

/work/repo contains an empty project and a written specification, `SPEC.md` (about 300 lines), for a small SQL
engine: CREATE/INSERT/SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE/DROP, expressions with three-valued logic, scalar functions, aggregates,
GROUP BY/HAVING, joins, subqueries (also correlated), UNION, transactions, a write-ahead log file format, and a
command line front end. Implement it as `/work/repo/minisql.py` in pure Python 3.12, standard library only. You may
NOT use the `sqlite3` module (or any other SQL engine) in your implementation: it must be your own parser and
executor, and the grader reads the source. This statement is also
saved as /work/repo/TASK.md.

## What you have
- `SPEC.md`: the exact semantics. Where it is silent inside the supported subset, SQLite 3.46 behaviour is the reference.
  The `sqlite3` module and `sqlite3` command line tool exist in this container so that you can compare behaviour
  yourself while developing (as an oracle for your own tests, not inside `minisql.py`).
- `tests/public_cases.json` and `tests/run_public.py`: about 30 example cases in the grader's own format (a sample of
  the hidden suite's style, with expected results). Run `python3 tests/run_public.py -v` from /work/repo.
- `minisql.py`: a stub with the API names.

## Grading
- A hidden suite of a few hundred cases, grouped into 15 milestones from easy to hard (expressions, tables and
  basic queries, WHERE, ORDER/LIMIT/DISTINCT, functions, aggregates, GROUP BY, UPDATE/DELETE, constraints and error
  codes, transactions, joins, subqueries and UNION, correlated subqueries, the log file format, the command line).
  Each case is a script of statements with expected rows / row counts / error codes, run against a fresh database in
  its own Python process (30 s limit). A milestone passes only when every case in it passes; the grade is the
  fraction of milestones passed (the fraction of individual cases is recorded too). Partial credit is the point: do
  the easy groups first, then keep going through the harder ones.
- Row order is only compared when the query has ORDER BY; unordered results are compared as multisets. Floats are
  compared with a tiny tolerance but int and float are different types.
- The log file is also checked independently: the grader parses the file your `Database` wrote and replays it with
  SQLite, and opens files produced by the reference implementation (including torn tails) with your code.

## Rules
- Work in /work/repo. The result must be importable as `import minisql` with the working directory containing
  `minisql.py`. Helper modules are fine if they live next to it, but a single file is simplest.
- You may work for several hours. Your context window is limited and will be summarized as you work: keep design
  notes, decisions and the list of known gaps in /work/repo/NOTES.md, and put your own tests under /work/repo/tests/.
- When you believe you are done, write many extra queries of your own, run each through both your engine and the
  `sqlite3` module, and fix every difference inside the supported subset; re-read SPEC.md section by section.
